questions.stemHtml: A 25 y/o male presents to the emergency after a sports injury involving a sudden pivot on his left knee. An MRI reveals a tear in the anterior cruciate ligament (ACL). Which statement regarding the knee ligaments is true?

options.label: B
options.text: Lateral collateral ligament attaches to the patella.

options.label: C
options.text: The medial meniscus is wider anteriorly.

options.label: D
options.text: PCL prevents anterior displacement of the femur.

questions.answerText: PCL prevents anterior displacement of the femur.
questions.solution: a" data-dictid="1ba6a9cfe11692777181950edd7a6d">anterior displacement of the femur and posterior displacement of the tibia when the knee is flexed, making it essential for knee stability. Extracapsular Ligaments Intracapsular Ligaments Ligamentum Patellae: Attaches from the lower border of the patella to the tibial tuberosity. Continuation of the quadriceps femoris tendon. Lateral (Fibular) Collateral Ligament: (Option B ruled out) Cord-like structure attaching from the femur's lateral condyle to the fibula's head. The Popliteus tendon is located between this ligament and the lateral meniscus. Medial (Tibial) Collateral Ligament: Flat band connecting the medial condyle of the femur to the medial surface of the tibia. Firmly attached to the medial meniscus. Oblique Popliteal Ligament: Tendinous expansion from the semimembranosus muscle, strengthening the posterior capsule. Medial Meniscus Semicircular, wider posteriorly than anteriorly. (Option C ruled out) The peripheral margin adheres to the deep part of the tibial collateral ligament; posterior fibres are continuous with the transverse ligament. Lateral Meniscus Circular. The posterior end is attached to the medial condyle of the femur via two meniscofemoral ligaments; separated from the fibular collateral ligament by the popliteus tendon. Anterior Cruciate Ligament (ACL): (Option A ruled out) It attaches to the anterior intercondylar area of the tibia and ascends to the posterior part of the lateral femoral condyle. Prevents posterior displacement of the femur and anterior displacement of the tibia when the knee is flexed. It is extrasynovial. Posterior Cruciate Ligament (PCL): It attaches to the posterior intercondylar area of the tibia and extends to the anterior part of the medial femoral condyle. Prevents anterior displacement of the femur and posterior displacement of the tibia when the knee is flexed. It is extrasynovial. Intercondylar area attachments Classification of Ligaments and Menisci by Location and Synovial Relation Intracapsular and Intrasynovial: Menisci (lie within the joint capsule and are bathed by synovial fluid). Intracapsular but Extrasynovial: Cruciate ligaments (located within the joint capsule but outside the synovial cavity). Extracapsular and Extrasynovial: Collateral ligaments (outside both the joint capsule and synovial cavity). @Neet_pg_bot

Extracapsular Ligaments

Intracapsular Ligaments
  • Ligamentum Patellae:
    • Attaches from the lower border of the patella to the tibial tuberosity.
    • Continuation of the quadriceps femoris tendon.
  • Lateral (Fibular) Collateral Ligament: (Option B ruled out)
    • Cord-like structure attaching from the femur's lateral condyle to the fibula's head.
    • The Popliteus tendon is located between this ligament and the lateral meniscus.
  • Medial (Tibial) Collateral Ligament:
    • Flat band connecting the medial condyle of the femur to the medial surface of the tibia.
    • Firmly attached to the medial meniscus.
  • Oblique Popliteal Ligament:
    • Tendinous expansion from the semimembranosus muscle, strengthening the posterior capsule.
  • Medial Meniscus
    • Semicircular, wider posteriorly than anteriorly. (Option C ruled out)
    • The peripheral margin adheres to the deep part of the tibial collateral ligament; posterior fibres are continuous with the transverse ligament.
  • Lateral Meniscus
    • Circular.
    • The posterior end is attached to the medial condyle of the femur via two meniscofemoral ligaments; separated from the fibular collateral ligament by the popliteus tendon.
  • Anterior Cruciate Ligament (ACL): (Option A ruled out)
    • It attaches to the anterior intercondylar area of the tibia and ascends to the posterior part of the lateral femoral condyle.
    • Prevents posterior displacement of the femur and anterior displacement of the tibia when the knee is flexed.
    • It is extrasynovial.
  • Posterior Cruciate Ligament (PCL):
    • It attaches to the posterior intercondylar area of the tibia and extends to the anterior part of the medial femoral condyle.
    • Prevents anterior displacement of the femur and posterior displacement of the tibia when the knee is flexed.
    • It is extrasynovial.

Intercondylar area attachments

 

Classification of Ligaments and Menisci by Location and Synovial Relation

  • Intracapsular and Intrasynovial: Menisci (lie within the joint capsule and are bathed by synovial fluid).
  • Intracapsular but Extrasynovial: Cruciate ligaments (located within the joint capsule but outside the synovial cavity).
  • Extracapsular and Extrasynovial: Collateral ligaments (outside both the joint capsule and synovial cavity).

questions.solution: p; Explanation: Demographic Burden Refers to the increase in the proportion of the dependent population relative to the economically productive population. It signifies the societal challenge of supporting a larger dependent population, which typically occurs due to aging demographics. Demographic Bonus A phase in a nation's demographic evolution in which the proportion of the dependent population relative to the working-age population declines. This is often associated with economic growth opportunities as more people are in the workforce than dependents. Demographic Window: Refers to a period in a nation's demographic structure when the proportion of the population in the working-age group is at its highest. questions.stem: A 3-year-old girl presents with developmental delay, ataxic gait, and frequent inappropriate laughter. Genetic testing reveals a deletion in the 15q11-q13 region of the maternal chromosome. Which of the following conditions is most likely?
questions.stemHtml: A 3-year-old girl presents with developmental delay, ataxic gait, and frequent inappropriate laughter. Genetic testing reveals a deletion in the 15q11-q13 region of the maternal chromosome. Which of the following conditions is most likely?
questions.solution: customMeta" data-dictid="12e1e505d8169277720189a6ea33dd">uniparental disomy. Genomic imprinting is an epigenetic phenomenon (alteration in DNA without any change in nucleotide sequence) where certain genes are expressed in a parent-of-origin-specific manner. The maternal or paternal allele is silenced, while the other is expressed. This gene silencing is commonly linked to DNA methylation . Angelman syndrome (AS) is caused by the loss of function of the maternally inherited UBE3A gene in the 15q11-q13 region. This can occur through various mechanisms, including deletions, mutations, or imprinting defects. The key features of AS include developmental delay, ataxic gait, and inappropriate laughter, all of which are present in this patient. {{caption_text}} Feature Angelman Syndrome Prader-Willi Syndrome Genetic Cause Deletion or mutation of the maternal UBE3A gene on chromosome 15q11-q13. Deletion or mutation of the paternal region on chromosome 15q11-q13, or maternal uniparental disomy. Developmental Milestones Severe developmental delay; speech is often minimal or absent. Mild to moderate developmental delay; speech and motor skills are delayed. Physical Features Microcephaly, frequent smiling/laughter, ataxia, seizures. Hypotonia, obesity, short stature, small hands and feet. Behavioral Characteristics Happy demeanor, hyperactivity, fascination with water. Food-seeking behavior, temper tantrums, compulsive behaviors. Intellectual Disability Severe to profound intellectual disability. Mild to moderate intellectual disability. Seizures Common and often severe. Rare, typically not a prominent feature. Growth Patterns Normal or mildly affected growth; often underweight. Hyperphagia leading to obesity if not managed. Sleep Disturbances Frequent, often severe sleep disturbances. Common, often associated with excessive daytime sleepiness. Disorder with maternal uniparental disomy(Option A) : While PWS also involves the 15q11-q13 region, it results from the loss of paternally expressed genes in this region with maternal disomy. PWS presents with hypotonia, obesity, and cognitive impairment, which don't match the given clinical picture. {{caption_text}} Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome (BWS) (Option C) : BWS is an overgrowth disorder caused by dysregulation of imprinted genes on chromosome 11p15.5. It typically presents with macrosomia, macroglossia, and an increased risk of embryonal tumors, which are not described in this case. {{caption_text}} Silver-Russell syndrome (SRS) (Option D) : SRS is a growth restriction disorder associated with imprinting defects on chromosomes 7 and 11. It is characterized by intrauterine growth restriction, postnatal growth failure, and body asymmetry, which don't align with the presented symptoms. {{caption_text}} @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
customMeta" data-dictid="12e1e505d8169277720189a6ea33dd">uniparental disomy.
  • Genomic imprinting is an epigenetic phenomenon (alteration in DNA without any change in nucleotide sequence) where certain genes are expressed in a parent-of-origin-specific manner.
  • The maternal or paternal allele is silenced, while the other is expressed.
  • This gene silencing is commonly linked to DNA methylation.

    • Angelman syndrome (AS) is caused by the loss of function of the maternally inherited UBE3A gene in the 15q11-q13 region.

    • This can occur through various mechanisms, including deletions, mutations, or imprinting defects.
    • The key features of AS include developmental delay, ataxic gait, and inappropriate laughter, all of which are present in this patient.

     

    Feature

    Angelman Syndrome

    Prader-Willi Syndrome

    Genetic Cause

    Deletion or mutation of the maternal UBE3A gene on chromosome 15q11-q13.

    Deletion or mutation of the paternal region on chromosome 15q11-q13, or maternal uniparental disomy.

    Developmental Milestones

    Severe developmental delay; speech is often minimal or absent.

    Mild to moderate developmental delay; speech and motor skills are delayed.

    Physical Features

    Microcephaly, frequent smiling/laughter, ataxia, seizures.

    Hypotonia, obesity, short stature, small hands and feet.

    Behavioral Characteristics

    Happy demeanor, hyperactivity, fascination with water.

    Food-seeking behavior, temper tantrums, compulsive behaviors.

    Intellectual Disability

    Severe to profound intellectual disability.

    Mild to moderate intellectual disability.

    Seizures

    Common and often severe.

    Rare, typically not a prominent feature.

    Growth Patterns

    Normal or mildly affected growth; often underweight.

    Hyperphagia leading to obesity if not managed.

    Sleep Disturbances

    Frequent, often severe sleep disturbances.

    Common, often associated with excessive daytime sleepiness.


     

    Disorder with maternal uniparental disomy(Option A):

    • While PWS also involves the 15q11-q13 region, it results from the loss of paternally expressed genes in this region with maternal disomy.
    • PWS presents with hypotonia, obesity, and cognitive impairment, which don't match the given clinical picture.

    Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome (BWS) (Option C):

    • BWS is an overgrowth disorder caused by dysregulation of imprinted genes on chromosome 11p15.5.
    • It typically presents with macrosomia, macroglossia, and an increased risk of embryonal tumors, which are not described in this case.

     

    Silver-Russell syndrome (SRS) (Option D):

    • SRS is a growth restriction disorder associated with imprinting defects on chromosomes 7 and 11.
    • It is characterized by intrauterine growth restriction, postnatal growth failure, and body asymmetry, which don't align with the presented symptoms.

questions.solution: strong>encapsulated yeast cells on India ink staining, most commonly caused by Cryptococcus neoformans . The recommended initial treatment is a combination of amphotericin B and flucytosine for induction therapy, followed by fluconazole for consolidation. Fungal meningitis: Causes Cryptococcus neoformans (most common) Candida Histoplasma Blastomyces Coccidioides Sporothrix Risk factors Immunocompromised patients Clinical features Headache Altered mental status, lethargy Fever Neck stiffness Nausea and vomiting. Investigations Lumbar Puncture: Low glucose and high protein levels. White cell count can be normal or higher than 20 microL and have a lymphocyte predominance. Treatment (Options A, C & D ruled out) LAMB (Liposomal Amphotericin-B) and 5-Fluorocytosine (Flucytosine) for 2 weeks Fluconazole is given subsequently for 8-10 weeks. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 3 year old child presents with swelling and pain in the region of the parotid gland, accompanied by ear discharge. Examination of the external auditory canal (EAC) reveals signs of infection. Which bony anatomical structure is responsible for the spread of infection between the EAC and the parotid gland?
questions.stemHtml: A 3 year old child presents with swelling and pain in the region of the parotid gland, accompanied by ear discharge. Examination of the external auditory canal (EAC) reveals signs of infection. Which bony anatomical structure is responsible for the spread of infection between the EAC and the parotid gland?
questions.solution: e: A deficiency in the anteroinferior bony EAC, present in some children under four and occasionally into adulthood. It allows infection to spread between the parotid gland and the EAC. (Option B) Fissures of Santorini: Two gaps in the cartilage of the outer EAC that allow infection to pass between the parotid glands and the EAC. Isthmus: A narrowing in the bony EAC, about 6 mm lateral to the tympanic membrane. It is not an opening but a constriction in the canal. (Option C) Tympanic membrane (Option D) : The tympanic membrane separates the external ear from the middle ear and is not involved in spreading infections to the parotid gland. Mastoid Air Cells (Option A) : Mastoid air cells are a series of air-filled spaces located within the mastoid process of the temporal bone, adjacent to the middle ear. While infections in the middle ear (otitis media) can spread to the mastoid air cells (causing mastoiditis), they do not directly connect the EAC to the parotid gland. Thus, they are not responsible for the spread of infection between these two areas. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
e: A deficiency in the anteroinferior bony EAC, present in some children under four and occasionally into adulthood.
  • It allows infection to spread between the parotid gland and the EAC. (Option B)
  • Fissures of Santorini: Two gaps in the cartilage of the outer EAC that allow infection to pass between the parotid glands and the EAC.
  • Isthmus: A narrowing in the bony EAC, about 6 mm lateral to the tympanic membrane. It is not an opening but a constriction in the canal. (Option C)

    • Tympanic membrane (Option D):

    • The tympanic membrane separates the external ear from the middle ear and is not involved in spreading infections to the parotid gland.

    Mastoid Air Cells (Option A):

    • Mastoid air cells are a series of air-filled spaces located within the mastoid process of the temporal bone, adjacent to the middle ear.
    • While infections in the middle ear (otitis media) can spread to the mastoid air cells (causing mastoiditis), they do not directly connect the EAC to the parotid gland.
    • Thus, they are not responsible for the spread of infection between these two areas.

questions.solutionHtml:
ong>

Halothane is contraindicated in patients with ischaemic heart disease.

  • Halothane decreases cardiac output, BP, and PR
  • Halothane causes hypotension by direct myocardial depression
  • Halothane causes bradycardia by blunting carotid body receptor response
  • Halothane is a common inhalational agent used in the respiratory system (due to maximum bronchodilation) while Isoflurane is the common inhalational agent used in CNS and CVS

Central Nervous System:

  • Inhalational agents are CNS depressant
  • They reduce cerebral metabolic rate
  • Commonly used inhalational agent is isoflurane
  • They increase the cerebral blood flow thereby increasing the ICP, so they are avoided in head injury and neurosurgery (maximum with halothane)
  • Isoflurane is an inhalational agent of choice in head injury as it decreases the ICP (Option A)
  • Most epileptogenic agent: Enflurane (increases ICP and also causes epilepsy)

Respiratory system

  • Almost all inhalational agents cause bronchodilation (Option C)
  • Reduces the Respiratory rate
  • Causes decreased mucociliary function (except ether)
  • Maximum bronchodilation is seen with halothane, therefore 2nd best inhalational agent for bronchial asthma is halothane.
  • Best inhalational agent for bronchial asthma: Sevoflurane (Option D)

Cardiovascular system

  • Reduces heart rate, BP, and systemic vascular resistance
  • Halothane increases the sensitivity of the myocardium toward catecholamines
  • Halothane, isoflurane, enflurane - prolong QT interval

Gastrointestinal system:

  • Reduces the liver blood flow
  • Halothane hepatitis: maximally metabolized produces trifluoroacetic acid as an end product that reacts with liver cells (immunologically) causing acute fulminant hepatic necrosis.

Uterus:

  • All agents are good uterine relaxants so there is a high chance of PPH

questions.solutionHtml:
ient align with the diagnostic criteria for substance dependence according to DSM-5, as given below:
  1. Impaired control: The patient uses opioids in larger amounts than intended and has made unsuccessful attempts to cut down.
  2. Social impairment: She has given up hobbies and often misses work due to opioid use.
  3. Continued use despite consequences: She continues to use despite legal problems (arrested for stealing prescription pads) and negative impacts on her life.

 

Dependence:

Dependence is a state where a person exhibits both physical and psychological symptoms related to substance use.

 

Type of Dependence

Definition

Behavioral Dependence

Focuses on substance-seeking behaviors and the patterns of pathological use.

Physical Dependence

Refers to the physiological effects that result from repeated episodes of substance use.

Psychological Dependence

Also called habituation, characterized by a persistent or occasional craving to avoid dysphoria.

 

Substance Use Disorder Criteria (DSM-5):

The criteria for diagnosing substance dependence can be grouped into four main categories:

  1. Impaired Control:
    • Using larger amounts or for longer periods than intended
    • Persistent desire or unsuccessful efforts to cut down or control use
    • Spending excessive time obtaining, using, or recovering from the substance
    • Experiencing intense cravings or urges to use the substance
  2. Social Impairment:
    • Failing to fulfill major role obligations due to substance use
    • Continuing use despite persistent social or interpersonal problems
    • Giving up important activities because of substance use (Progressive Neglect)
  3. Risky Use:
    • Recurrent use in physically hazardous situations
    • Continued use despite knowledge of physical or psychological problems caused or exacerbated by the substance (Persistence)
  4. Pharmacological Criteria:
    • Tolerance: Needing increased amounts to achieve desired effects or experiencing reduced effects with the same amount
    • Withdrawal: Experiencing characteristic withdrawal symptoms or using the substance to relieve withdrawal.

 

(Option A): While the patient likely meets the criteria for opioid dependence, the scenario doesn't provide explicit evidence of tolerance or withdrawal.

(Option B) is incorrect because the patient's presentation goes beyond abuse and meets the criteria for dependence.

(Option D) is incorrect because the origin of use (medically sanctioned) doesn't prevent a diagnosis of dependence. The pattern of use, loss of control, and continued use despite significant problems all point to dependence rather than mere misuse.

Considering 2 grams of bleaching powder (calcium hypochlorite) is needed per cubic meter of water for effective disinfection, how much bleaching powder is required to disinfect this well?
questions.solution: n: 1. Calculate the volume of the well : Volume of a cylinder = π × (radius)² × height (or) V= π x (diameter/2)² x height Radius = Diameter / 2 = 1.5 meters / 2 = 0.75 meters Height = Depth of the well = 10 meters Volume = π × (0.75 meters)² × 10 meters → Volume ≈ 3.14 × 0.5625 × 10 → Volume ≈ 17.67 cubic meters 2. Calculate the amount of bleaching powder needed : Bleaching powder required = Volume of the well × Amount of bleaching powder per cubic meter ⇒ 17.67 cubic meters × 2 grams per cubic meter Bleaching powder required ≈ 35.33 grams Rounding off, the required amount of bleaching powder is approximately 35 grams. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
n:

1. Calculate the volume of the well:

  • Volume of a cylinder = π × (radius)² × height (or) V= π x (diameter/2)² x height
  • Radius = Diameter / 2 = 1.5 meters / 2 = 0.75 meters
  • Height = Depth of the well = 10 meters

Volume = π × (0.75 meters)² × 10 meters

→ Volume ≈ 3.14 × 0.5625 × 10

→ Volume ≈ 17.67 cubic meters

2. Calculate the amount of bleaching powder needed:

  • Bleaching powder required = Volume of the well × Amount of bleaching powder per cubic meter

⇒ 17.67 cubic meters × 2 grams per cubic meter

  • Bleaching powder required ≈ 35.33 grams

Rounding off, the required amount of bleaching powder is approximately 35 grams.

questions.stemHtml: Match the following: 1) Pneumocystis pneumonia a) 2) Blastomycosis b) 3) Aspergillus c) 4) Measles d)
questions.solution: li>Pneumocystis jirovecii is an opportunistic fungus that causes Pneumocystis pneumonia (PCP). PCP primarily affects immunocompromised individuals . Gomori’s methenamine silver (GMS) staining is the method of choice to demonstrate the cysts of P. jirovecii. The cysts resemble black-coloured crushed ping-pong balls against the green background. Blastomycosis: Blastomycosis is a fungal infection caused by Blastomyces dermatitidis found in moist soil. Morphology: In the normal host, the lung lesions of blastomycosis are suppurative granulomas. Macrophages have a limited ability to ingest and kill B. dermatitidis, and the persistence of the yeast cells leads to the recruitment of neutrophils . In tissue, B. dermatitidis is a round, 5- to 15-μm yeast cell divided by broad-based budding. It has a thick, double-contoured cell wall and visible nuclei. Aspergillus: Aspergillosis is an invasive and allergic disease caused by a hyaline mould named Aspergillus. Glucocorticoid use is the most important risk factor for aspergillosis. Pulmonary aspergillosis is the most common form. KOH (10%) mount or histopathological staining of specimens reveals characteristic narrow septate hyaline hyphae with acute angle branching. Measles: The measles virus is a single-stranded RNA virus of the Paramyxoviridae family. It causes measles, an acute, highly contagious childhood disease characterised by fever and respiratory symptoms followed by a typical maculopapular rash. Virus isolation: Cytopathic effect may be observed after 7–10 days of inoculation into cell lines characterised by multinucleated giant cells (Warthin-Finkeldey cells) containing intranuclear and intracytoplasmic inclusion bodies. It can cause giant-cell pneumonitis (Hecht’s pneumonia) in immunocompromised children and HIV-infected people. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: ictid="7644c201051692777194859abcd534">pancytopenia is probably due to bone marrow suppression caused by his anti-cancer drugs. Vincristine, a vinca alkaloid, specifically targets cells during the M phase (mitosis). It binds to tubulin and inhibits microtubule formation. questions.stem: A 45-year-old professional singer presents with complaints of vocal fatigue and difficulty producing high-pitched sounds for the last 3 months. She denies any difficulty in swallowing or breathing. On laryngoscopic examination, no significant abnormalities are seen, and one vocal cord appears to be in normal resting position while other vocal cord is in abducted position . What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.stemHtml: A 45-year-old professional singer presents with complaints of vocal fatigue and difficulty producing high-pitched sounds for the last 3 months. She denies any difficulty in swallowing or breathing. On laryngoscopic examination, no significant abnormalities are seen, and one vocal cord appears to be in normal resting position while other vocal cord is in abducted position . What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.solution: SLN palsy Explanation: In this scenario, the patient is a professional singer who reports difficulty with high-pitched sounds, which is a hallmark of unilateral SLN palsy . The external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve innervates the cricothyroid muscle , which tenses the vocal cords, crucial for producing high-pitched sounds. In unilateral SLN palsy, the patient does not experience breathing or swallowing difficulties, and laryngoscopic examination may appear normal. Unilateral SLN Palsy Motor Loss: Cricothyroid muscle - decreased ability to tense the vocal cord. Sensory Loss: Above the vocal cord on the affected side. Vocal Cord Position: The affected vocal cord appears shortened and wavy ; may exhibit flapping due to loss of tension. Other Features: Askew position of the glottis with the anterior commissure rotated towards the healthy side. Voice changes such as weakness and inability to raise pitch, affecting singing ability. Treatment: Primarily voice therapy to improve vocal function and manage symptoms. Bilateral SLN Palsy Motor Loss: Both cricothyroid muscles - bilateral loss of vocal cord tension. Sensory Loss: Above the vocal cords bilaterally. Vocal Cord Position: Both vocal cords may be shortened and lack tension , potentially leading to difficulties with voice production. Other Features: Inhalation of food and secretions resulting in coughing and choking . The voice is weak and husky . Treatment: Tracheostomy with a cuffed tube and esophageal feeding tube, if aspiration is severe. Epiglottopexy (reversible) - close laryngeal inlet - to protect the lungs from aspiration. Voice pitch improvement through surgical approximation of the thyroid and cricoid cartilages. Bilateral SLN palsy (Option A): The patient would have more pronounced symptoms, including a monotonous voice, significant difficulty with high-pitched sounds, and aspiration due to poor sensation in the upper larynx. Unilateral RLN palsy (Option C) Causes hoarseness and, on laryngoscopy, shows one vocal cord in a paramedian position . In contrast, this patient's difficulty is specifically related to high-pitched sounds , pointing to SLN involvement rather than RLN. Bilateral RLN palsy (Option D): It is a severe condition that typically results in stridor or significant respiratory difficulty due to both vocal cords being fixed in the paramedian position. The absence of breathing or swallowing problems in this patient rules out bilateral RLN palsy. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
SLN palsy

 

Explanation:

  • In this scenario, the patient is a professional singer who reports difficulty with high-pitched sounds, which is a hallmark of unilateral SLN palsy.
  • The external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve innervates the cricothyroid muscle, which tenses the vocal cords, crucial for producing high-pitched sounds.
  • In unilateral SLN palsy, the patient does not experience breathing or swallowing difficulties, and laryngoscopic examination may appear normal.

 

Unilateral SLN Palsy

  • Motor Loss: Cricothyroid muscle - decreased ability to tense the vocal cord.
  • Sensory Loss: Above the vocal cord on the affected side.
  • Vocal Cord Position: The affected vocal cord appears shortened and wavy; may exhibit flapping due to loss of tension.
  • Other Features:
    • Askew position of the glottis with the anterior commissure rotated towards the healthy side.
    • Voice changes such as weakness and inability to raise pitch, affecting singing ability.
  • Treatment: Primarily voice therapy to improve vocal function and manage symptoms.

 

Bilateral SLN Palsy

  • Motor Loss: Both cricothyroid muscles - bilateral loss of vocal cord tension.
  • Sensory Loss: Above the vocal cords bilaterally.
  • Vocal Cord Position: Both vocal cords may be shortened and lack tension, potentially leading to difficulties with voice production.
  • Other Features:
    • Inhalation of food and secretions resulting in coughing and choking.
    • The voice is weak and husky.
  • Treatment:
    • Tracheostomy with a cuffed tube and esophageal feeding tube, if aspiration is severe.
    • Epiglottopexy (reversible) - close laryngeal inlet - to protect the lungs from aspiration.
    • Voice pitch improvement through surgical approximation of the thyroid and cricoid cartilages.

 

Bilateral SLN palsy (Option A):

  • The patient would have more pronounced symptoms, including a monotonous voice, significant difficulty with high-pitched sounds, and aspiration due to poor sensation in the upper larynx.

 

Unilateral RLN palsy (Option C)

  • Causes hoarseness and, on laryngoscopy, shows one vocal cord in a paramedian position.
  • In contrast, this patient's difficulty is specifically related to high-pitched sounds, pointing to SLN involvement rather than RLN.

 

Bilateral RLN palsy (Option D):

  • It is a severe condition that typically results in stridor or significant respiratory difficulty due to both vocal cords being fixed in the paramedian position.
  • The absence of breathing or swallowing problems in this patient rules out bilateral RLN palsy.

questions.stem: Which muscle is the first to regain function after muscle relaxation?
questions.stemHtml: Which muscle is the first to regain function after muscle relaxation?
questions.solution: > The diaphragm , a central muscle involved in breathing, receives a high blood supply, making it one of the first to recover after muscle relaxants wear off. The fast recovery of the diaphragm is important for restoring normal respiratory function following surgery. Triceps (Option A): The triceps, located in the upper arm, are peripherally situated and recover later than centrally located muscles. The slower return of function in muscles like the triceps is due to their lower blood supply and distant location from central circulation. Adductor pollicis (Option B): Located in the hand, this peripheral muscle tends to recover more slowly because it has lower blood flow compared to central muscles. It is useful for monitoring complete neuromuscular recovery. Quadriceps (Option C): Quadriceps exhibit a slower recovery because they are more distant from central circulation and have less blood flow compared to muscles like the diaphragm. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stemHtml: A 60-year-old man presents with complaints of fatigue, shortness of breath, and swelling in his legs. He has had a history of intermittent facial flushing and diarrhea for the past several years. Physical examination reveals a new heart murmur. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.solution: p; Explanation: The patient's history of facial flushing, diarrhea, and a newly detected heart murmur, coupled with symptoms of right-sided heart failure (such as leg swelling and shortness of breath), strongly points toward carcinoid heart disease. Carcinoid heart disease is a complication of carcinoid syndrome, which results from the release of serotonin and other vasoactive substances by a carcinoid tumor. Pathophysiology: Plaque-like deposits composed of smooth muscle cells, myofibroblasts, extracellular matrix and an overlying endothelial layer which lead to valve dysfunction. Valvular dysfunction can lead to edema, ascites and right-sided heart failure. Pulmonary heart disease primarily affects the right side of the heart. Within the right heart, the tricuspid valve is the first to be affected, followed by the pulmonary valve. Regurgitant lesions are more common than stenotic lesions. @Neet_pg_bot

p;

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT a chain-breaking antioxidant?
questions.stemHtml: Which of the following is NOT a chain-breaking antioxidant?
questions.solution: Correct answer: Option D- Glutathione Peroxidase Glutathione Peroxidase is a preventive antioxidant, not a chain-breaking antioxidant. Antioxidants are substances that help control and reduce lipid peroxidation by neutralizing free radicals, which can cause cellular damage. Classification of Antioxidants: 1. Preventive Antioxidants: Reduce the rate of chain initiation. Examples: Glutathione Peroxidase (Option D) Catalase Selenium 2. Chain-Breaking Antioxidants (Option A, B and C ruled out): Interfere with chain propagation by stabilizing free radicals. Examples: α-Tocopherol (Vitamin E) β-Carotene (Vitamin A) Vitamin C Superoxide Dismutase (SOD) @Neet_pg_bot

Glutathione Peroxidase is a preventive antioxidant, not a chain-breaking antioxidant.

Antioxidants are substances that help control and reduce lipid peroxidation by neutralizing free radicals, which can cause cellular damage.

Classification of Antioxidants:

1. Preventive Antioxidants:

  • Examples:

2. Chain-Breaking Antioxidants (Option A, B and C ruled out):

  • Examples:

MAC Definition:

The concentration of the general anaesthetic in the alveoli of the lung that produces unresponsiveness to the surgical incision in 50% of patients.

 

Nitrous oxide (Option A): It has a very high MAC value (105%) and is not potent enough to be used as a sole anaesthetic agent.

 

Desflurane (Option C): It has a MAC value of around 6%, so it is less potent than sevoflurane. However, it has a very rapid onset and offset, making it suitable for short procedures and outpatient surgeries.

 

Halothane (Option D): It has a very low MAC value (0.75%), indicating high potency, but it is associated with significant side effects, including hepatotoxicity, and is less commonly used today.

questions.stem: A 12-year-old child presents with headaches, visual disturbances, and delayed growth. An MRI of the brain reveals a 3 cm cystic mass with calcifications. The growth was found to be encapsulated and multiloculated. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.stemHtml: A 12-year-old child presents with headaches, visual disturbances, and delayed growth. An MRI of the brain reveals a 3 cm cystic mass with calcifications. The growth was found to be encapsulated and multiloculated. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.solution: mas are benign tumours arising from vestigial remnants of the Rathke pouch. They commonly occur in the suprasellar region and often present as encapsulated and multiloculated cystic masses with calcifications. The cysts contain cholesterol-rich, thick brownish-yellow fluid (compared to machine oi). It has 2 histological variants: Adamantinomatous and papillary. The common presentations include headaches and visual disturbances like bitemporal hemianopia due to optic chiasma compression, while children present with growth retardation due to pituitary hypofunction and GH deficiency. Oligodendroglioma (Option A): Typically affects adults (30–50 years old). Commonly located in the cerebral hemispheres , not suprasellar. Calcifications can be present, but they are intra-axial and not cystic or multiloculated. Endocrine symptoms are rare . Meningioma (Option B): Rare in children; typically seen in middle-aged to older adults . Usually extra-axial , solid , may calcify but are not cystic or multiloculated. Often found incidentally unless very large. It does not cause hormonal dysfunction in children. Pituitary Adenoma(Option D): Unlikely in a child. Pituitary adenomas are rare in children. Typically, adenomas cause endocrine symptoms, but visual changes in children from adenomas are uncommon. Less likely to be calcified or multiloculated. Usually, solid tumours are not cystic. @Neet_pg_bot

The common presentations include headaches and visual disturbances like bitemporal hemianopia due to optic chiasma compression, while children present with growth retardation due to pituitary hypofunction and GH deficiency.

 

Oligodendroglioma (Option A): Typically affects adults (30–50 years old). Commonly located in the cerebral hemispheres, not suprasellar. Calcifications can be present, but they are intra-axial and not cystic or multiloculated. Endocrine symptoms are rare. 

Meningioma (Option B): Rare in children; typically seen in middle-aged to older adults. Usually extra-axial, solid, may calcify but are not cystic or multiloculated. Often found incidentally unless very large. It does not cause hormonal dysfunction in children. 

Pituitary Adenoma(Option D): Unlikely in a child. Pituitary adenomas are rare in children. Typically, adenomas cause endocrine symptoms, but visual changes in children from adenomas are uncommon. Less likely to be calcified or multiloculated. Usually, solid tumours are not cystic.

questions.stemHtml: A 6-month-old infant is brought to the clinic by their parents reporting that their infant is not meeting developmental milestones, such as rolling over or sitting up. On examination, the infant has eczema and a noticeable musty odor. Hair and skin pigmentation appear lighter. Which of the following enzymes is deficient in this infant?
questions.solution: g> Explanation: The infant’s symptoms, like failure to meet developmental milestones, eczema, a musty odor, and lighter hair and skin pigmentation, are characteristic of Phenylketonuria (PKU) . PKU is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by a defect in the enzyme phenylalanine hydroxylase (PAH). This enzyme deficiency disrupts the body's ability to metabolize the amino acid phenylalanine, leading to its accumulation in the body. Deficiency in tyrosinase (Option B) causes albinism. It does not typically present with a musty odor or developmental delays. Deficiency in tyrosine aminotransferase (Option C) can cause tyrosinemia type 2, which primarily affects the eyes and skin but does not present with a musty odor or developmental delays Deficiency in 4-HPPD (Option D) is less common and typically does not include the musty odor. It causes tyrosinemia type- 3 (Hawkinsuria) with a swimming pool (chlorine) odor. @Neet_pg_bot

MID UPPER ARM CIRCUMFERENCE (MUAC)

Definition
  • MUAC - used to assess the nutritional status of children aged 6 months to 5 years. (Option B)

Procedure
  • Ensure the child is standing straight with their left arm free of clothing. The arm should be bent at a right angle.

  • Use a MUAC tape to wrap around the marked midpoint of the arm. The tape should be snug but not tight enough to pinch the skin.
  • Record the measurement at the zero mark of the tape.

Shakir’s Tape

Rapid weight loss can lead to fat mobilisation and subsequent fat embolism, resulting in vascular obstruction and ischemia, which are key contributors to osteonecrosis. Causes of Osteonecrosis Trauma: Fractures or dislocations disrupt blood supply, especially in the femoral neck, scaphoid, and talus. Corticosteroid Use: High-dose steroids cause fat cell swelling and intravascular stasis, leading to bone ischemia Alcohol Abuse: Chronic alcohol use leads to fat embolism and marrow swelling, causing venous stasis. Sickle Cell Disease: Sickled red cells obstruct blood vessels, leading to ischemia and bone death. Gaucher’s Disease: Lipid accumulation in bone marrow causes vascular compression and ischemia Thrombophilia: Increased blood clotting tendency leads to capillary thrombosis, causing bone necrosis. Antiphospholipid Antibodies: As seen in SLE, these antibodies promote clot formation, leading to ischemia. Fat Embolism: Fat emboli block capillaries, causing endothelial damage and thrombosis. Venous Stasis: Marrow swelling increases intraosseous pressure, leading to venous blockage and ischemia. Dysbaric Osteonecrosis: . Rapid decompression (e.g., in divers) causes gas bubbles in vessels, leading to bone necrosis. Pregnancy: Hormonal changes and fatty liver can decrease fibrinolysis, increasing clot formation. Radiation Exposure: Radiation damages blood vessels, leading to poor blood flow and bone necrosis Postoperative autoimmune response leading to synovitis (Option A): Postoperative autoimmune response leading to synovitis typically presents with widespread joint symptoms and inflammatory markers rather than localised bone marrow oedema seen in osteonecrosis Osteoporosis due to nutritional deficiencies (Option C): Nutritional deficiencies can lead to weakened bones, but they neither cause intermittent swelling nor osteonecrosis as suggested by the MRI findings. Bed rest post-surgery (Option D): Prolonged immobility could cause stiffness but is less likely to explain significant pain and swelling and the osteonecrosis suggested by the MRI findings. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: What is the primary function of the Rapoport-Luebering Shunt in red blood cells?
questions.stemHtml: What is the primary function of the Rapoport-Luebering Shunt in red blood cells?

options.label: B
options.text: To produce 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate, which regulates oxygen binding to hemoglobin

options.label: D
options.text: To facilitate the conversion of glucose to glucose-6-phosphate

questions.answerText: To produce 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate, which regulates oxygen binding to hemoglobin
questions.solution: 3041692777182726fdec300">2,3-bisphosphoglycerate (2,3-BPG) through a series of enzymatic reactions involving 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate (1,3-BPG). Formation of 1,3-BPG: In glycolysis, glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate is converted to 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate by the enzyme glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase. This reaction involves the addition of an inorganic phosphate and the reduction of NAD+ to NADH. Conversion to 2,3-BPG: In the Rapoport-Luebering Shunt, 1,3-BPG is converted to 2,3-BPG by the enzyme bisphosphoglycerate mutase. This reaction shifts the phosphate group from the first carbon to the second carbon of the glycerate molecule, forming 2,3-BPG. Conversion of 2,3-BPG to 3-phosphoglycerate: 2,3-BPG can be hydrolyzed to 3-phosphoglycerate by the enzyme 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate phosphatase. This reaction removes a phosphate group, resulting in the formation of 3-phosphoglycerate, which then re-enters the glycolytic pathway. The Rapoport-Luebering Shunt does not generate ATP; it bypasses an ATP-generating step in glycolysis (Option A) . The conversion of pyruvate to lactate is a function of lactate dehydrogenase and is not related to the Rapoport-Luebering Shunt (Option C) . The conversion of glucose to glucose-6-phosphate is catalyzed by hexokinase or glucokinase and occurs at the very beginning of glycolysis, unrelated to the Rapoport-Luebering Shunt (Option D) . @Neet_pg_bot

  • Formation of 1,3-BPG:
    • In glycolysis, glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate is converted to 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate by the enzyme glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase.
    • This reaction involves the addition of an inorganic phosphate and the reduction of NAD+ to NADH.
  • Conversion to 2,3-BPG:
    • In the Rapoport-Luebering Shunt, 1,3-BPG is converted to 2,3-BPG by the enzyme bisphosphoglycerate mutase.
    • This reaction shifts the phosphate group from the first carbon to the second carbon of the glycerate molecule, forming 2,3-BPG.
  • Conversion of 2,3-BPG to 3-phosphoglycerate:
    • 2,3-BPG can be hydrolyzed to 3-phosphoglycerate by the enzyme 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate phosphatase.
    • This reaction removes a phosphate group, resulting in the formation of 3-phosphoglycerate, which then re-enters the glycolytic pathway.

 

The Rapoport-Luebering Shunt does not generate ATP; it bypasses an ATP-generating step in glycolysis (Option A).

 

The conversion of pyruvate to lactate is a function of lactate dehydrogenase and is not related to the Rapoport-Luebering Shunt (Option C).

 

The conversion of glucose to glucose-6-phosphate is catalyzed by hexokinase or glucokinase and occurs at the very beginning of glycolysis, unrelated to the Rapoport-Luebering Shunt (Option D).

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man presents with progressive hearing loss in his right ear. Audiometry reveals sensorineural hearing loss, and an MRI shows no abnormalities in the cochlear nerve. A defect in converting mechanical sound vibrations into electrical signals is suspected. Which of the following structures is most likely affected?
questions.stemHtml: A 45-year-old man presents with progressive hearing loss in his right ear. Audiometry reveals sensorineural hearing loss, and an MRI shows no abnormalities in the cochlear nerve. A defect in converting mechanical sound vibrations into electrical signals is suspected. Which of the following structures is most likely affected?
questions.solution: anation: The patient presents with sensorineural hearing loss, typically caused by damage to the inner ear or the neural pathways responsible for hearing. Given the defect in converting mechanical sound vibrations into electrical signals, the likely issue lies in the Organ of Corti, where the hair cells transduce sound vibrations into electrical impulses. The Organ of Corti , located on the basilar membrane inside the cochlea, contains the hair cells responsible for the hearing transduction mechanism . When sound waves are transmitted through the ear and reach the inner ear, they cause vibrations of the basilar membrane , which bend stereocilia on the hair cells. Inner hair cells are arranged in a single row, while outer hair cells form three to four rows. Inner hair cells transmit auditory stimuli to the brain, while outer hair cells modulate inner hair cell function to enhance sound sensitivity and clarity. This bending opens ion channels, generating electrical impulses. These impulses are sent through the auditory nerve to the brain, where they are interpreted as sound. Oval window (Option A) is a membrane-covered opening between the middle and inner ear. It plays a role in the mechanical conduction of sound by transmitting vibrations from the stapes to the fluid in the cochlea but is in converting those vibrations into electrical signals. Tympanic membrane (Option C) vibrates in response to sound and transmits from the external ear to the ossicles of the middle ear. Damage leads to conductive hearing loss but doesn't affect sound transduction. Stapes footplate (Option D): This structure amplifies sound waves but involves the conductive hearing process, not sensorineural conversion. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stemHtml: A 29-year-old woman with a history of self-harm, chronic emptiness, and unstable relationships often alternates between idealizing and devaluing others. What defense mechanism is most commonly observed in this disorder?
questions.solution: nation: Splitting is a common defense mechanism in borderline personality disorder, where individuals view people or situations as either all good or all bad, contributing to their unstable relationships. BORDERLINE PERSONALITY DISORDER: General Characteristics More common in females than in males. Persons with BPD are often in a state of crisis, with frequent mood swings, shifting from being argumentative to depressed, and later feeling numb. They can experience short-lived psychotic episodes and their behavior is highly unpredictable, Self-Destructive Behaviors Repetitive self-destructive acts such as wrist slashing or self-mutilation, often to elicit help from others, express anger, or numb overwhelming emotions. Interpersonal Relationships Individuals with BPD have tumultuous interpersonal relationships, feeling both dependent on others and hostile toward them when frustrated. They cannot tolerate being alone and prefer companionship, even in unhealthy relationships. Identity and Emotional Experience Chronic feelings of emptiness, boredom, and a lack of a consistent sense of identity (identity diffusion) are common, with some complaining of feeling depressed despite fluctuating moods. Distorted Relationships Relationships are distorted, with others seen as either "all good" or "all bad" due to splitting , leading to idealization or devaluation of people. Defense Mechanism Projective identification is a common defense mechanism, where patients project unacceptable aspects of themselves onto others, inducing them to play the projected role. Treatment Dialectical behaviour therapy. Mentalization based therapy. Transference: Focussed Psychotherapy. Pharmacotherapy: Antipsychotics, antidepressants, mood stabilizers like carbamazepine. Sublimation (Option A) is a mature defense mechanism where individuals redirect unacceptable impulses or emotions into socially acceptable behaviors or activities. Rationalization (Option C) involves explaining away or justifying behaviors or feelings to make them seem more acceptable or less distressing. Displacement (Option D) involves shifting emotions from a threatening target to a safer one, such as expressing anger toward a friend instead of an authority figure. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
nation:
  • Splitting is a common defense mechanism in borderline personality disorder, where individuals view people or situations as either all good or all bad, contributing to their unstable relationships.

 

BORDERLINE PERSONALITY DISORDER:

 

General Characteristics

  • More common in females than in males.
  • Persons with BPD are often in a state of crisis, with frequent mood swings, shifting from being argumentative to depressed, and later feeling numb.
  • They can experience short-lived psychotic episodes and their behavior is highly unpredictable,

 

Self-Destructive Behaviors

  • Repetitive self-destructive acts such as wrist slashing or self-mutilation, often to elicit help from others, express anger, or numb overwhelming emotions.

 

Interpersonal Relationships

  • Individuals with BPD have tumultuous interpersonal relationships, feeling both dependent on others and hostile toward them when frustrated.
  • They cannot tolerate being alone and prefer companionship, even in unhealthy relationships.

 

Identity and Emotional Experience

  • Chronic feelings of emptiness, boredom, and a lack of a consistent sense of identity (identity diffusion) are common, with some complaining of feeling depressed despite fluctuating moods.

 

Distorted Relationships

  • Relationships are distorted, with others seen as either "all good" or "all bad" due to splitting, leading to idealization or devaluation of people.

 

Defense Mechanism

  • Projective identification is a common defense mechanism, where patients project unacceptable aspects of themselves onto others, inducing them to play the projected role.

 

Treatment

  • Dialectical behaviour therapy.
  • Mentalization based therapy.
  • Transference: Focussed Psychotherapy.
  • Pharmacotherapy: Antipsychotics, antidepressants, mood stabilizers like carbamazepine.

 

Sublimation (Option A) is a mature defense mechanism where individuals redirect unacceptable impulses or emotions into socially acceptable behaviors or activities.

Rationalization (Option C) involves explaining away or justifying behaviors or feelings to make them seem more acceptable or less distressing.

Displacement (Option D) involves shifting emotions from a threatening target to a safer one, such as expressing anger toward a friend instead of an authority figure.

Boundaries

Explanation:

The management of pressure sores depends on the stage and severity of the wound.

For a stage III pressure sore, conservative management is typically the initial approach, with surgery reserved for more advanced cases or when conservative measures fail.

 

Conservative management includes:

1. Pressure relief: Repositioning the patient every 2-3 hours

2. Wound care: Cleaning and dressing the wound

3. Nutritional support: Ensuring adequate protein and calorie intake

4. Hydrocolloid dressings: These maintain a moist environment, promote autolytic debridement, and protect the wound

 

Surgical management is considered for:

1. Stage III and IV pressure sores that fail to heal with conservative measures

2. Exposed bone, tendon, or joint

3. Undermining, tunneling, or sinus tract formation

 

Surgical options include:

Immediate surgical debridement (Option A) is incorrect as it's too aggressive for initial management.

Negative pressure wound therapy (Option C) is typically used after debridement and is not the first-line treatment.

Flap reconstruction (Option D) is a surgical option reserved for more advanced cases or when conservative measures fail.

An abdominal X-ray shows a dilated loop of small intestine near the pancreas. Which of the following is the most likely imaging sign observed on the X-ray in this patient?
questions.solution: The patient’s clinical presentation of severe epigastric pain radiating to the back and elevated lipase levels strongly suggests acute pancreatitis . Sentinel loop sign is a classic X-ray finding in acute pancreatitis, showing a dilated loop of the small intestine near the pancreas due to localized ileus caused by the inflammation. Acute Pancreatitis Clinical Diagnosis (Requires 2 of 3): Abdominal pain is strongly suggestive of acute pancreatitis. Serum amylase and/or lipase level at least 3 times the upper limit of normal. Imaging findings characteristic of acute pancreatitis. X-ray Features • Sentinel loop sign (Option C) : ◦ Dilated loop of small intestine near the inflamed pancreas due to localized ileus. ◦ Significance : Early indicator of acute pancreatitis on X-ray. Sentinel loop sign • Colon cut-off sign : ◦ Abrupt termination of gas in the colon at the splenic flexure, with collapsed distal colon loops. ◦ Significance : Suggests localized pancreatic inflammation, causing colonic spasm as an indirect sign of acute pancreatitis Investigations of Choice: Contrast-enhanced CT (CECT) : Primary tool for assessing pancreatic necrosis, peripancreatic inflammation, fluid collections, and complications. Most reliable for staging and detecting complications. May underestimate necrosis if done in the first 24 hours. Morphological Types (Revised Atlanta Classification 2008): Interstitial oedematous pancreatitis :: Mild form with pancreatic oedema and swelling but no necrosis. Necrotising pancreatitis : Severe form involving pancreatic parenchymal necrosis, associated with higher morbidity and mortality. Colon cut-off sign (Option A) : Seen in acute pancreatitis, it indicates abrupt gas cut-off in the colon at the splenic flexure but doesn't explain small intestine dilation abdominal X-ray findings. Pneumoperitoneum (Option B) : Refers to free air under the diaphragm, often due to bowel perforation, and is not linked to acute pancreatitis. Ground-glass opacity (Option D) : Typically seen in lung imaging (e.g., pneumonia, ARDS), not related to pancreatitis or abdominal X-ray findings. @Neet_pg_bot

The patient’s clinical presentation of severe epigastric pain radiating to the back and elevated lipase levels strongly suggests acute pancreatitis. Sentinel loop sign is a classic X-ray finding in acute pancreatitis, showing a dilated loop of the small intestine near the pancreas due to localized ileus caused by the inflammation.

Acute Pancreatitis

Clinical Diagnosis (Requires 2 of 3):

  1. Abdominal pain is strongly suggestive of acute pancreatitis.
  2. Serum amylase and/or lipase level at least 3 times the upper limit of normal.
  3. Imaging findings characteristic of acute pancreatitis.

 

X-ray Features

 

• Sentinel loop sign (Option C): 

◦ Dilated loop of small intestine near the inflamed pancreas due to localized ileus.

◦ Significance: Early indicator of acute pancreatitis on X-ray.

Sentinel loop sign

• Colon cut-off sign: 

◦ Abrupt termination of gas in the colon at the splenic flexure, with collapsed distal colon loops.

◦ Significance: Suggests localized pancreatic inflammation, causing colonic spasm as an indirect sign of acute pancreatitis

Investigations of Choice:

  • Contrast-enhanced CT (CECT): Primary tool for assessing pancreatic necrosis, peripancreatic inflammation, fluid collections, and complications.
    • Most reliable for staging and detecting complications.
    • May underestimate necrosis if done in the first 24 hours.

Morphological Types (Revised Atlanta Classification 2008):

  1. Interstitial oedematous pancreatitis:: Mild form with pancreatic oedema and swelling but no necrosis.
  2. Necrotising pancreatitis: Severe form involving pancreatic parenchymal necrosis, associated with higher morbidity and mortality.

Colon cut-off sign (Option A): Seen in acute pancreatitis, it indicates abrupt gas cut-off in the colon at the splenic flexure but doesn't explain small intestine dilation abdominal X-ray findings.

Pneumoperitoneum (Option B): Refers to free air under the diaphragm, often due to bowel perforation, and is not linked to acute pancreatitis.

Ground-glass opacity (Option D): Typically seen in lung imaging (e.g., pneumonia, ARDS), not related to pancreatitis or abdominal X-ray findings.

Explanation:

The introjection of lost objects is a part of the psychodynamic theory of depression, while the cognitive triad is a component of the cognitive theory, involving self-perception, environment, and the future.

Psychosocial Theories of Depression

Life Events and Environmental Stress

  • Stressful life events often precede the first episode of mood disorders.
  • Initial stress may lead to long-lasting biological changes, increasing the risk for future episodes even without further stressors.

 

Psychodynamic Theories

  • Early disturbances in the infant-mother relationship predispose to depression.
  • Depression is linked to real or imagined loss of significant objects.
  • Introjection of lost objects serves as a defense mechanism.
  • Feelings of love and hate toward the lost object result in self-directed anger.

 

Cognitive Theory

  • Depression arises from cognitive distortions known as depressogenic schemata.
  • Cognitive Triad (by Aaron Beck):
    • Worthlessness: Negative self-perception. (Option A)
    • Helplessness: Perception of the environment as hostile and demanding. (Option B)
    • Hopelessness: Expectation of suffering and failure in the future. (Option C)
  • Therapy focuses on modifying these cognitive distortions.

 

Learned Helplessness

  • Developed from studies showing that exposure to uncontrollable stressors (e.g., electric shocks in dogs) leads to passive behavior.
  • Humans may internalize helplessness and lose self-esteem after adverse events.
  • Improvement in depression involves learning a sense of control and mastery over one’s environment.

 

Evolutionary Theory

  • Depression is viewed as an adaptive response to perceived environmental threats.
  • Withdrawal from social situations and decreased activity may serve as protective mechanisms.

questions.solution: 21β-hydroxylase deficiency leads to reduced cortisol and aldosterone production, causing elevated ACTH and increased production of androgens, resulting in virilization and ambiguous genitalia. Congenital Adrenal Hyperplasia (CAH) Definition: Group of genetic disorders affecting adrenal glands, causing enzyme deficiencies in steroid biosynthesis. Effects: Disruption in cortisol and aldosterone production, leading to various symptoms. Prevalence: Most common deficiency is 21β-hydroxylase deficiency (90%+ cases). 21β-Hydroxylase Deficiency Impact: Reduced cortisol and aldosterone production. Consequence: Increased ACTH secretion. Masculinization in females, hypospadias in males. (Option C) 17α-Hydroxylase deficiency Caused by mutated CYP17 gene. Prevents sex hormone production. 21β-hydroxylase deficiency leads to reduced cortisol and aldosterone production, causing elevated ACTH and increased production of androgens, resulting in virilization and ambiguous genitalia.

 

Congenital Adrenal Hyperplasia (CAH)

  • Definition: Group of genetic disorders affecting adrenal glands, causing enzyme deficiencies in steroid biosynthesis.
  • Effects: Disruption in cortisol and aldosterone production, leading to various symptoms.
  • Prevalence: Most common deficiency is 21β-hydroxylase deficiency (90%+ cases).

21β-Hydroxylase Deficiency

  • Impact: Reduced cortisol and aldosterone production.
  • Consequence: Increased ACTH secretion. (Option B)
  • Result: Increased precursor steroids converted to androgens → Virilization.

Other Enzyme Deficiencies in CAH

Enzyme Deficiency

Description

Symptoms/Consequences

Cholesterol desmolase deficiency

Fatal in utero, prevents placental progesterone synthesis.

Death before birth.

Steroidogenic acute regulatory (StAR) protein deficiency

Known as congenital lipoid adrenal hyperplasia. Prevents cholesterol movement into mitochondria.

Low steroid production, female genitalia regardless of genetic sex.

3β-Hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase deficiency

Increases DHEA secretion (weak androgen).

Masculinization in females, hypospadias in males. (Option C)

17α-Hydroxylase deficiency

Caused by mutated CYP17 gene. Prevents sex hormone production.

Female external genitalia, hypertension, hypokalemia due to high 11-deoxycorticosterone. (Option D- not early virilization)

11β-Hydroxylase deficiency

Increased 11-deoxycortisol and 11-deoxycorticosterone secretion.

Virilization, hypertension due to salt and water retention. (Option A)

Treatment

  • Glucocorticoid treatment: Recommended for all virilizing forms of CAH.
    • Purpose: Addresses glucocorticoid deficit.
    • Effect: Inhibits ACTH secretion, reducing androgen and steroid production.

questions.solution: specific antibodies (DSAs) in the serum, along with histological evidence of glomerulitis or peritubular capillaritis observed in biopsy samples. Additionally, linear C4d staining in peritubular capillaries serves as a critical marker for confirming the diagnosis. Acute Humoral Rejection (AHR): Definition Significant complication in organ transplantation, particularly in kidney transplants. Characterized by donor-specific antibodies (DSAs) targeting the vascular endothelium, leading to tissue injury and graft dysfunction - Acute process (Option A & C ruled out) Mechanisms of AHR: Binding of DSAs to donor HLA molecules activates the complement system, resulting in: Capillary Injury : Damage to peritubular capillaries is a hallmark of AHR. C4d Deposition : A key diagnostic marker ; approximately 30% of acute rejection biopsies show widespread C4d staining. Histological Features : May include neutrophilic infiltration, glomerulitis, and fibrinoid necrosis in severe cases. Diagnostic Criteria Combination of clinical presentation, serological testing, and histopathological findings: Histologic Evidence : Glomerulitis or peritubular capillaritis. Antibody Interaction : Linear C4d staining indicates recent antibody interaction with vascular endothelium. Detection of DSAs : Presence of DSAs in serum confirms diagnosis. Symptoms Acute Elevation in Creatinine : Noted within days to weeks post-transplant. Fever and Malaise Graft Tenderness Treatment: (Option D ruled out) Plasmapheresis : Removes circulating antibodies. Intravenous Immunoglobulin (IVIG) : Modulates immune responses. Rituximab : Targets CD20 on B cells to reduce antibody production. Eculizumab : A complement inhibitor effective in severe AHR cases. @Neet_pg_bot

specific antibodies (DSAs) in the serum, along with histological evidence of glomerulitis or peritubular capillaritis observed in biopsy samples. Additionally, linear C4d staining in peritubular capillaries serves as a critical marker for confirming the diagnosis.

 

Acute Humoral Rejection (AHR):

  • Definition
    • Significant complication in organ transplantation, particularly in kidney transplants.
    • Characterized by donor-specific antibodies (DSAs) targeting the vascular endothelium, leading to tissue injury and graft dysfunction - Acute process (Option A & C ruled out)
  • Mechanisms of AHR:
    • Binding of DSAs to donor HLA molecules activates the complement system, resulting in:
      • Capillary Injury: Damage to peritubular capillaries is a hallmark of AHR.
      • C4d Deposition: A key diagnostic marker; approximately 30% of acute rejection biopsies show widespread C4d staining.
      • Histological Features: May include neutrophilic infiltration, glomerulitis, and fibrinoid necrosis in severe cases.
  • Diagnostic Criteria
    • Combination of clinical presentation, serological testing, and histopathological findings:
      • Histologic Evidence: Glomerulitis or peritubular capillaritis.
      • Antibody Interaction: Linear C4d staining indicates recent antibody interaction with vascular endothelium.
      • Detection of DSAs: Presence of DSAs in serum confirms diagnosis.
  • Symptoms
    • Acute Elevation in Creatinine: Noted within days to weeks post-transplant.
    • Fever and Malaise
    • Graft Tenderness
  • Treatment: (Option D ruled out)
    • Plasmapheresis: Removes circulating antibodies.
    • Intravenous Immunoglobulin (IVIG): Modulates immune responses.
    • Rituximab: Targets CD20 on B cells to reduce antibody production.
    • Eculizumab: A complement inhibitor effective in severe AHR cases.

    • M = Methyl red test

    • V = VP test

    • C = Citrate utilization test

      • E. coli → + + – –

      • Klebsiella → – – + +

    Escherichia coli (Option A): Although it can appear pink on MacConkey agar due to lactose fermentation, E. coli is indole-positive and urease-negative, ruling it out.

     

    Proteus mirabilis (Option C): Proteus species are typically non-lactose fermenting and would not appear pink on MacConkey agar. They also do not appear mucoid.

questions.solution: Explanation: A cross-sectional study is used to determine the prevalence of a disease in a population at a specific time. It is also known as a snapshot of the total population. Here it is cross-sectional study because it calculates prevalence of a disease and relies on primary data, i.e., researcher collects the data himself. To assess the incidence, a Cohort study (Option A) starts by determining whether risk factors are present. Case-control study (Option C) determines whether an exposure is associated with an outcome. It starts with diseased and non-diseased. An Ecological study (Option D) compares exposure and disease frequency in a series of populations. The unit of study is population. Ecological study uses secondary data. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: nbsp; Explanation: The symptoms and examination findings, including hip pain radiating to the groin and thigh, worsened by activity and restricted motion, indicate avascular necrosis of the femoral head , commonly following an intracapsular neck of femur fracture. The inferior gluteal artery primarily supplies the gluteal region and does not contribute significantly to the blood supply of the femoral head. Therefore, it is not typically involved in AVN associated with neck of femur fractures. Blood supply to the femoral head and neck Blood Supply Source Description Retinacular Vessels Major supply, derived from the medial and lateral circumflex femoral arteries (branches of the deep femoral artery). Forms an extensive network along the femoral neck. Intraosseous Cervical Vessels Secondary source, providing additional vascular support through small penetrating vessels along the femoral neck. Artery of Ligamentum Teres Tertiary source, also called the foveolar artery. Supplies the femoral head via the ligamentum teres. Important in younger patients or in cases of trauma. Obturator Artery Provides minor support through its acetabular branch. Primarily supplies the medial thigh muscles but contributes to anastomoses around the hip joint. @Neet_pg_bot

Blood Supply Source

Description

Retinacular Vessels
  • Major supply, derived from the medial and lateral circumflex femoral arteries (branches of the deep femoral artery).
  • Forms an extensive network along the femoral neck.

Intraosseous Cervical Vessels
  • Secondary source, providing additional vascular support through small penetrating vessels along the femoral neck.

Artery of Ligamentum Teres
  • Tertiary source, also called the foveolar artery.

  • Provides minor support through its acetabular branch.
  • Primarily supplies the medial thigh muscles but contributes to anastomoses around the hip joint.

questions.stemHtml: A 65-year-old patient presents with a 2.5 cm ulcerative lesion on the right side of his lower lip confirmed as squamous cell carcinoma. Which of the following statements is correct regarding the primary lymphatic drainage and surgical management of this lesion?

options.label: A
options.text: Drains to submental nodes; level I neck dissection is sufficient.

options.label: B
options.text: Drains to ipsilateral submandibular nodes; levels I-III neck dissection is recommended.

options.label: C
options.text: High risk of contralateral metastasis; bilateral neck dissection is needed.

options.label: D
options.text: Drains to preauricular and parotid nodes; requires superficial parotidectomy.

questions.answerText: Drains to ipsilateral submandibular nodes; levels I-III neck dissection is recommended.
questions.solution: Explanation: The lymphatic drainage of the lower lip is primarily to the submental (level IA) and submandibular (level IB) nodes . There's a significant risk of occult nodal metastasis for a lesion of this size, especially one close to the commissure. Therefore, a selective neck dissection, including levels I-III on the ipsilateral side, is typically recommended even in N0. Management 1. Early Stage (T1-T2N0): Wide local excision with 1 cm margins Consider elective neck dissection for tumors >2 cm or >4 mm depth Reconstruction: Primary closure, local flaps, or skin grafts 2. Advanced Stage (T3-T4 or N+): Wide local excision with ≥1 cm margins Neck dissection (comprehensive or selective based on nodal status) Complex reconstruction (local/regional flaps, free tissue transfer) Adjuvant radiotherapy or chemoradiotherapy based on pathological findings 3. Management of the Neck: Elective neck dissection for high-risk tumors (>2 cm, >4 mm depth) Therapeutic neck dissection for clinically positive nodes Levels typically addressed: I-III for N0 neck, I-V for N+ neck @Neet_pg_bot

Explanation:

  • The lymphatic drainage of the lower lip is primarily to the submental (level IA) and submandibular (level IB) nodes.
  • There's a significant risk of occult nodal metastasis for a lesion of this size, especially one close to the commissure.
  • Therefore, a selective neck dissection, including levels I-III on the ipsilateral side, is typically recommended even in N0.

 

 

 

Management

1. Early Stage (T1-T2N0):

  • Wide local excision with 1 cm margins
  • Consider elective neck dissection for tumors >2 cm or >4 mm depth
  • Reconstruction: Primary closure, local flaps, or skin grafts

 

2. Advanced Stage (T3-T4 or N+):

  • Wide local excision with ≥1 cm margins
  • Neck dissection (comprehensive or selective based on nodal status)
  • Complex reconstruction (local/regional flaps, free tissue transfer)
  • Adjuvant radiotherapy or chemoradiotherapy based on pathological findings
 

3. Management of the Neck:

  • Elective neck dissection for high-risk tumors (>2 cm, >4 mm depth)
  • Therapeutic neck dissection for clinically positive nodes
  • Levels typically addressed: I-III for N0 neck, I-V for N+ neck

ass="customMeta" data-dictid="d69566338f1692777189ff10521054">histopathology showing intramacrophagic yeast form and (LPCB) mount showing numerous hyaline hyphae with few tuberculate macroconidia (arrows) and many smooth-walled oval microconidia are pointing towards a diagnosis of disseminated histoplasmosis.

Histoplasmosis

Diagnosis

Microscopy:

  • Stained smears of the specimens show small intra- and extracellular yeast cells
 

Culture:

  • Blood agar and Sabouraud agar show characteristic growth
  • White, cottony, mycelial growth with large, thick-walled, spherical spores with tuberculate (finger-like projections)
 

Serodiagnosis:

  • Antibody titers increase in progressive disease
  • Antigen tests on urine and serum are helpful for immunocompromised individuals.

Skin Test:

  • Delayed hypersensitivity to histoplasmin confirms exposure

Treatment

Amphotericin-B (Option B) for two to four weeks, followed by a year of itraconazole (Option A ruled out)

Fluconazole (Option C ruled out): It is usually reserved for less severe infections or maintenance therapy after initial treatment with more potent antifungals like amphotericin-B. 

Surgical resection (Option D ruled out): It may be considered for localised infections or complications like abscesses, but it is not appropriate as a primary treatment strategy for disseminated histoplasmosis.

questions.stemHtml: A 45-year-old woman presents with a 6-month history of muscle weakness, fatigue, and frequent urination. Her blood pressure is 160/95 mmHg. Investigations: Serum K+: 2.8 mEq/L, Serum Na+: 148 mEq/L, Plasma aldosterone: 35 ng/dL, Plasma renin activity: 0.2 ng/mL/h. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.solution: Conn's syndrome, also known as primary hyperaldosteronism, which is due to autonomous overproduction of aldosterone, usually from an adrenal adenoma. It is characterised by resistant hypertension, hypokalemia, and metabolic alkalosis. Causes: Aldosterone-producing adenoma (Conn's adenoma) - Most common. Bilateral adrenal hyperplasia. Symptoms often include muscle weakness, fatigue, headaches, and frequent urination. Laboratory findings: Elevated plasma aldosterone levels Suppressed plasma renin activity High aldosterone-to-renin ratio Treatment involves surgical removal of the adenoma and the use of mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists, such as spironolactone and eplerenone. Role of Aldosterone : It acts on the collecting duct to – Increase sodium reabsorption via epithelial sodium channels (ENaC). Enhance potassium secretion through potassium channels (ROMK). Bartter's syndrome(Option A) It is a genetic disorder,childhood-onset, affecting the kidneys, leading to abnormalities in electrolyte reabsorption. Typically presents with low blood pressure, hypokalemia, metabolic alkalosis, elevated renin levels, and high urinary calcium excretion (hypercalciuria). Gitelman's syndrome :( Option B) A genetic disorder affects the distal convoluted tubule of the kidney, leading to hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia, and metabolic alkalosis. Typically presents with low or normal blood pressure and low urinary calcium excretion (hypocalciuria). Liddle's syndrome(Option D) It is a genetic disorder caused by the increased activity of epithelial sodium channels (ENaC), leading to sodium retention and potassium excretion. It has low aldosterone and renin levels and typically presents with hypertension. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
Conn's syndrome, also known as primary hyperaldosteronism, which is due to autonomous overproduction of aldosterone, usually from an adrenal adenoma.
  • It is characterised by resistant hypertension, hypokalemia, and metabolic alkalosis.
  • Causes:
    • Aldosterone-producing adenoma (Conn's adenoma) - Most common.
    • Bilateral adrenal hyperplasia.
  • Symptoms often include muscle weakness, fatigue, headaches, and frequent urination.
  • Laboratory findings:
    • Elevated plasma aldosterone levels
    • Suppressed plasma renin activity
    • High aldosterone-to-renin ratio
  • Treatment involves surgical removal of the adenoma and the use of mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists, such as spironolactone and eplerenone.

Role of Aldosterone: It acts on the collecting duct to –

  • Increase sodium reabsorption via epithelial sodium channels (ENaC).
  • Enhance potassium secretion through potassium channels (ROMK).

Bartter's syndrome(Option A)

  • It is a genetic disorder,childhood-onset, affecting the kidneys, leading to abnormalities in electrolyte reabsorption.
  • Typically presents with low blood pressure, hypokalemia, metabolic alkalosis, elevated renin levels, and high urinary calcium excretion (hypercalciuria).

Gitelman's syndrome:(Option B)

  • A genetic disorder affects the distal convoluted tubule of the kidney, leading to hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia, and metabolic alkalosis.
  • Typically presents with low or normal blood pressure and low urinary calcium excretion (hypocalciuria).

Liddle's syndrome(Option D)

  • It is a genetic disorder caused by the increased activity of epithelial sodium channels (ENaC), leading to sodium retention and potassium excretion.
  • It has low aldosterone and renin levels and typically presents with hypertension.
