questions.stemHtml: A 45-year-old man presents with symptoms of urinary obstruction, including difficulty in starting urination, weak urinary stream, and frequent urinary tract infections. On physical examination, he has a history of trauma to the pelvic region. A retrograde urethrogram (RGU) reveals a stricture in the anterior urethra measuring more than 2 cm. Which of the following is the most appropriate management option for this patient?

options.label: C
options.text: Excision and reconstruction with buccal mucosa

questions.answerText: Excision and reconstruction with buccal mucosa
questions.solution: osa Explanation: Urethroplasty (Surgical excision and reconstruction) is the gold standard for managing long strictures (greater than 2 cm). This surgical procedure involves removing the affected stricture segment and reconstructing the urethra using a graft taken from the buccal mucosa. Urethral Stricture Definition Abnormal narrowing of the urethra, causing partial or complete obstruction of urine flow, leading to discomfort and severe complications if untreated. Causes Trauma (Most common): Pelvic fractures, falls, accidents, or iatrogenic trauma from prolonged catheterization. Infections: STIs like gonorrhea and chlamydia causing urethritis. Medical Procedures : Urethral surgeries or radiation for pelvic cancers. Inflammatory Conditions: Chronic inflammation from conditions like lichen sclerosus. Investigations Posterior Urethral Stricture: Micturating Cystourethrogram (MCU) to visualize the posterior urethra and bladder during voiding. {{caption_text}} Anterior Urethral Stricture: Retrograde Urethrogram (RGU). {{caption_text}} Emergency Evaluation: Both RGU and MCU may be used in trauma cases or acute urinary retention. Management Urethral Dilation: Temporary relief with dilators, often leading to recurrence. (Option A) Optical Internal Urethrotomy (OIU): Endoscopic incision at the 12 o'clock position; effective for short bulbar strictures (<2 cm). (Option B) Urethroplasty: Surgical excision and reconstruction; the gold standard for recurrent or complex strictures (Option C) . Strictures up to 2 cm: Excision with end-to-end anastomosis. Strictures >2 cm: Excision and reconstruction with buccal mucosa, bladder mucosa, or penile skin. Urethral Stenting (Option D) involves placing a stent in the urethra to keep it open. While stenting can relieve obstruction temporarily, it is not a definitive treatment for strictures and may be associated with complications, such as infection and migration of the stent. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
osa

 

Explanation:

 

  • Urethroplasty (Surgical excision and reconstruction) is the gold standard for managing long strictures (greater than 2 cm).
  • This surgical procedure involves removing the affected stricture segment and reconstructing the urethra using a graft taken from the buccal mucosa.

 

Urethral Stricture

 

Definition

Abnormal narrowing of the urethra, causing partial or complete obstruction of urine flow, leading to discomfort and severe complications if untreated.

Causes

Trauma (Most common): Pelvic fractures, falls, accidents, or iatrogenic trauma from prolonged catheterization.

Infections: STIs like gonorrhea and chlamydia causing urethritis.

Medical Procedures: Urethral surgeries or radiation for pelvic cancers.

Inflammatory Conditions: Chronic inflammation from conditions like lichen sclerosus.

Investigations

Posterior Urethral Stricture: Micturating Cystourethrogram (MCU) to visualize the posterior urethra and bladder during voiding.

Anterior Urethral Stricture: Retrograde Urethrogram (RGU).


Emergency Evaluation: Both RGU and MCU may be used in trauma cases or acute urinary retention.

Management

Urethral Dilation: Temporary relief with dilators, often leading to recurrence. (Option A)

Optical Internal Urethrotomy (OIU): Endoscopic incision at the 12 o'clock position; effective for short bulbar strictures (<2 cm).(Option B)

Urethroplasty: Surgical excision and reconstruction; the gold standard for recurrent or complex strictures (Option C).

  • Strictures up to 2 cm: Excision with end-to-end anastomosis.

questions.solution: Amlodipine is a long-acting dihydropyridine CCB, and it would be an appropriate choice to achieve better blood pressure control in the long term. It can be used as an add-on therapy with other antihypertensive agents, and its once-daily dosing improves patient compliance. Mechanism of action of CCB (Dihydropyridines): It blocks the entry of calcium ions through the L-type calcium channels in vascular smooth muscle cells, causing vasodilation and a reduction in peripheral vascular resistance. Drug Use Rationale for Choice Nifedipine (Option A) Short-acting Primarily used for angina pectoris Not recommended for long-term hypertension management due to its short duration of action and potential for reflex tachycardia. Nicardipine (Option B) Short-acting Commonly used in the management of hypertensive emergencies and perioperative hypertension or severe hypertension in the intensive care unit. The short duration of action makes it less suitable for long-term hypertension management. Clevidipine (Option C) Ultra-short-acting Very short half-life makes it unsuitable for long-term hypertension management. Amlodipine (Option D) Long-acting. Recommended as a first-line or add-on therapy for the long-term management of hypertension Preferred choice due to its long duration of action (up to 24 hours), once-daily dosing, and effectiveness in lowering blood pressure with good tolerability. @Neet_pg_bot

Techniques To Eliminate Confounders

Method

Description

Matching


 
  • Cases are matched with the control and should be similar to the control in every possible variable that can affect the study's outcome except the disease in question.
  • Done in a case-control study.
  • Eliminates only the known confounders.

Restriction

  • Limits participation in the study to individuals who are similar in terms of confounders.

Randomisation

  • The technique where every participant will get an equal and known chance of being allocated to either the treatment group or the control group.
  • Eliminates both known and unknown confounders.

Stratification (Segregate)

  • Stratify the participants of the study or segregate them.

Standardisation

  • Adjusting the results to a standard population to control for confounding variables often used in rate comparisons
  • Eliminate or control the effect of age and gender.

Multivariate regression models

  • Used when there are multiple confounders.

questions.solution: a-1 antitrypsin deficiency is a genetic condition characterised by low levels or dysfunctional alpha-1 antitrypsin protein. Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency: It is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by mutations in the alpha-1 antitrypsin gene located on Chromosome 14 . The condition primarily affects the lungs, leading to panacinar emphysema and the liver, causing cirrhosis due to abnormal protein accumulation. Cystic fibrosis (Option A) is a genetic disorder caused by CFTR gene mutations, leading to thick mucus, chronic lung infections, and bronchiectasis. While it causes obstructive lung disease, emphysema is not typical. Asthma (Option B) is a chronic inflammatory condition causing reversible airway obstruction and episodic wheezing, coughing, and breathlessness. It does not typically result in emphysema or structural lung damage. Bronchiectasis (Option D) is a condition of permanently dilated bronchi due to chronic infections or inflammation. While it causes cough and sputum production, it does not primarily lead to emphysema. @Neet_pg_bot

  • While it causes obstructive lung disease, emphysema is not typical.

 

Asthma (Option B) is a chronic inflammatory condition causing reversible airway obstruction and episodic wheezing, coughing, and breathlessness.

  • It does not typically result in emphysema or structural lung damage.

 

Bronchiectasis (Option D) is a condition of permanently dilated bronchi due to chronic infections or inflammation.

  • While it causes cough and sputum production, it does not primarily lead to emphysema.

Orbital apex syndrome; optic nerve (Option B) : It is a symptom complex due to the involvement of structures present at the apex of the orbit (structures passing through the superior orbital fissure and the optic canal) So the cranial nerves involved are II, III, IV, V, and VI Optic nerve (II) involvement causes visual loss and afferent pupillary defect Tolosa Hunt syndrome; II, III, and IV nerves (Option C) : Painful ophthalmoplegia from granulomatous inflammation in cavernous sinus/superior orbital fissure. Typically involves III, IV, VI, and V1, vision loss is not a defining feature. anation:

Clinical manifestation of ptosis (III), ophthalmoplegia (III, IV, VI), sensory loss over the forehead, and absent corneal reflex (V1) point towards the diagnosis of this syndrome.

 

 

 

Orbital apex syndrome; optic nerve (Option B):

  • It is a symptom complex due to the involvement of structures present at the apex of the orbit (structures passing through the superior orbital fissure and the optic canal)
  • So the cranial nerves involved are II, III, IV, V, and VI
  • Optic nerve (II) involvement causes visual loss and afferent pupillary defect

  • This refers to isolated oculomotor nerve palsy (after orbital trauma or fracture).

rted on linagliptin, a DPP-4 inhibitor that requires no dosage adjustment for renal impairment in this patient with type-2 diabetes and end-stage kidney disease (eGFR = 30 mL/min/1.73 m2).

 

 

Dipeptidyl peptidase-4 (DPP-4) inhibitors:

MOA
  • Increase Incretin Levels: Prevents degradation of incretin hormones (GLP-1 and GIP)
  • Enhance Insulin Secretion from the pancreas in response to meals. (no risk of hypoglycemia)
  • Reduce Glucagon Secretion
  • Maintain neutral weight

Uses
  • Oral hypoglycemic drug (type-2 diabetes)

Drugs
  1. Linagliptin: Safe in renal failure
  2. Teneligliptin: Safe in renal failure
  3. Vildagliptin: Hepatotoxic
  4. Alogliptin
  5. Sitagliptin
  6. Saxagliptin: (Option B)
    1. Metabolised by CYP3A4, it has more drug interactions.
    2. Requires dose adjustment in renal impairment.
    3. Risk of congestive heart failure.

Side effects
  • Nausea and vomiting (most common)
  • Pancreatitis (lesser than GLP-1)
  • Risk of pancreatic and thyroid cancer (lesser than GLP-1)
  • Arthritis, Nasopharyngitis:
    • Increase interleukins and cytokines levels (similar structure to CD26)
  • Hypersensitivity reactions: Steven-Johnson syndrome, angioedema


 

Dapagliflozin (Option A), an SGLT-2 inhibitor, is not recommended for use to improve glycemic control in patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus whose eGFR is less than 45 mL/min/1.73 m2.

 

Exenatide (Option C), a GLP-1 analogue, is avoided in patients with end-stage renal disease or ischemic renal failure due to hypovolemia.

Explanation:

In this scenario, the patient has a 3 cm asymptomatic endometrioma and does not desire future fertility. According to current guidelines, Follow-up 6 monthly with transvaginal ultrasound (TVS) is the most appropriate management for endometrioma as surgical interventions are indicated only for cysts> 5cm.

Management of Endometrioma:

  • If the patient wants to conceive:
    • Expectant management is done, irrespective of the size of the endometrioma
  • If pregnancy is not desired:
    • Size < 5cm and Asymptomatic: Follow up six monthly / 1 yearly with TVS
    • Size >5cm: Laparoscopic cystectomy (Option A)
  • Total Abdominal Hysterectomy (Option B):
    • Done only in women > 40 years after completion of family.
    • Prevents the formation of new lesions and pain due to it.
  • Laparoscopy procedures include:
    • Adhesiolysis
    • Fulgration of implants
    • Laparoscopic uterosacral nerve ablation (LUNA)
  • Laparoscopic uterosacral nerve ablation (LUNA) (Option C): It involves disrupting nerve pathways to alleviate pain associated with endometriosis, particularly pelvic pain. It is not indicated for the management of ovarian endometriomas.
  • After surgical procedures, patients require medical management
    • Adolescents <16 years: OCPs
    • Adolescents >16 years: OCPs / GnRH Agonists
    • Adults: OCPs / GnRH Agonists / Progesterone

questions.solution: uo;s presentation, along with the linear distribution of nodules, is suggestive of sporotrichosis/ Rose Gardner’s disease caused by Sporothrix schenckii. It is a Subcutaneous fungal infection that typically occurs after the fungus is traumatically inoculated into the skin, often through thorn pricks, splinters, or scratches from contaminated plant materials. Enzymes secreted by fungus, such as serine & aspartate proteinases help in local invasion. Sporothrix schenckii has a tendency to spread along lymphatics . Risk factors: Walking barefoot, farmers & gardeners. It can also be caused by the Actinomycetes bacteria, where there is the formation of yellow/ sulphur granules and discharging sinuses. Madura foot: {{caption_text}} {{caption_text}} Histopathology of Actinomycotic mycetoma: {{caption_text}} Muriform bodies (Option C) are seen in chromoblastomycosis , which also occurs in farmers with a history of thorn or thistle pricks. It shows slow-growing, polymorphic, verrucous (m/c type) lesions and sclerotic bodies (muriform cells/medlar bodies). questions.stemHtml: A 45-year-old male is undergoing surgery and is given repeated doses of suxamethonium for muscle relaxation. After some time, his muscle response starts to fade despite continuous stimulation. This is most likely due to the development of a phase II block. Which of the following is not a characteristic feature of phase II block with suxamethonium?

options.label: A
options.text: It is associated with a fade in muscle response during repetitive nerve stimulation

options.label: B
options.text: It can be influenced by prolonged exposure to suxamethonium

options.label: C
options.text: It responds predictably to cholinesterase inhibitors like neostigmine

options.label: D
options.text: Fast-twitch muscle fibres are more susceptible to phase II block than slow-twitch fibres

questions.answerText: It responds predictably to cholinesterase inhibitors like neostigmine
questions.solution: ong>Explanation: The response to cholinesterase inhibitors is unpredictable and may even worsen the block. Phase II Block (accommodation): It occurs with continuous or repeated exposure to depolarizing muscle relaxants, particularly suxamethonium, and is characterised by a gradual fade in muscle response. (Option A ruled out) Mechanisms Behind Phase II Block: Prejunctional effects : High concentrations of suxamethonium can block prejunctional acetylcholine receptors (AChRs), affecting acetylcholine synthesis and release. Postjunctional effects : Fade may also stem from changes in postjunctional AChR sensitivity or kinetics, resulting in reduced response despite the continued presence of the relaxant. TOF of Phase II depolarizing block Factors Influencing Phase II Block: Duration of exposure : Prolonged exposure to suxamethonium increases the chance of developing Phase II block. (Option B ruled out) Drug concentration : Higher suxamethonium concentrations make Phase II block more likely. Muscle type : Fast-twitch muscle fibres are more susceptible to Phase II block than slow-twitch fibres. (Option D ruled out) Interaction with other agents : Anesthetics or other drugs can affect the development of Phase II block. Reversal of Phase II Block: Cholinesterase inhibitors (e.g., neostigmine) : Not recommended as the response is unpredictable and could worsen the block. (Option C) . @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
ong>Explanation:

The response to cholinesterase inhibitors is unpredictable and may even worsen the block.

 

Phase II Block (accommodation):

It occurs with continuous or repeated exposure to depolarizing muscle relaxants, particularly suxamethonium, and is characterised by a gradual fade in muscle response. (Option A ruled out)

Mechanisms Behind Phase II Block:

  • Prejunctional effects: High concentrations of suxamethonium can block prejunctional acetylcholine receptors (AChRs), affecting acetylcholine synthesis and release.
  • Postjunctional effects: Fade may also stem from changes in postjunctional AChR sensitivity or kinetics, resulting in reduced response despite the continued presence of the relaxant.

TOF of Phase II depolarizing block

 

Factors Influencing Phase II Block:

  • Duration of exposure: Prolonged exposure to suxamethonium increases the chance of developing Phase II block. (Option B ruled out)
  • Drug concentration: Higher suxamethonium concentrations make Phase II block more likely.
  • Muscle type: Fast-twitch muscle fibres are more susceptible to Phase II block than slow-twitch fibres. (Option D ruled out)
  • Interaction with other agents: Anesthetics or other drugs can affect the development of Phase II block.

Reversal of Phase II Block:

  • Cholinesterase inhibitors (e.g., neostigmine): Not recommended as the response is unpredictable and could worsen the block. (Option C).

"border-collapse:collapse; width:614px">

Types and Causes

  • STEC-HUS: Caused by E. coli O157 (Shiga toxin)
  • Atypical HUS: Caused by genetic mutations, immune issues, pregnancy, cancers, medications

Pathophysiology and Pathology

  • Shiga toxin damages blood vessels in kidneys and brain

Clinical Features

  • Typical HUS: Bloody diarrhea, decreased urine output, paleness, lethargy, seizures
  • Atypical HUS: No bloody diarrhea, High blood pressure, mild breathing difficulties (Option C).

Diagnosis and Laboratory Investigations

Triad:

  • Hemolytic anemia
  • Thrombocytopenia
  • Acute kidney injury
 

Blood tests: Anemia, low platelet count, elevated creatinine

Stool cultures for E. coli O157 in STEC-HUS

Complications

  • Acute: Seizures, stroke, heart failure, death
  • Chronic: Chronic kidney disease (CKD)

Differential Diagnosis

  • ITP: Affects platelets only, lacks hemolytic anemia and kidney injury (Option A).
  • DIC: Widespread clotting and bleeding, different clinical features (DIC) (Option B)

Treatment

  • Supportive care
  • Plasma exchange for aHUS
  • Antibiotics not recommended for STEC-HUS

Key Steps in ACLS Step Description 1. Early Recognition and Activation Identify cardiac arrest signs quickly and alert emergency services. 2. High-Quality Chest Compressions (Option C) Initiate compressions at a rate of 100-120 per minute, with a depth of at least 2 inches (5 cm) for adults, allowing full chest recoil. 3. questions.solutionHtml:
Steps

Advanced Cardiac Life Support (ACLS) is crucial for managing cardiac arrest and cardiovascular emergencies, following the 2016 guidelines.

Key Steps in ACLS

Step

Description

1. Early Recognition and Activation

Identify cardiac arrest signs quickly and alert emergency services.

2. High-Quality Chest Compressions (Option C)

Initiate compressions at a rate of 100-120 per minute, with a depth of at least 2 inches (5 cm) for adults, allowing full chest recoil.

3. Early Defibrillation (Option D ruled out)

Deploy an AED promptly; follow prompts for defibrillation if a shockable rhythm is present.

4. Airway Management (Option B ruled out)

Ensure airway patency using techniques like bag-mask ventilation or advanced airway placement; provide oxygen to support ventilation.

5. Drug Administration (Option A ruled out)

Administer epinephrine (1 mg every 3-5 minutes); consider antiarrhythmics like amiodarone for shock-resistant VF/pulseless VT.

6. Identify and Treat Reversible Causes

Assess for reversible causes ("H's and T's"):

Hypoxia

Hypovolemia

Acidosis (Hydrogen ion)

Hyper/hypokalemia

Hypothermia

Tension pneumothorax

Cardiac tamponade

Toxins

Thrombosis (pulmonary/coronary)

7. Post-Resuscitation Care

Provide comprehensive care after return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC), including monitoring and supportive therapies.

8. Continuous Quality Improvement

Assess and enhance resuscitation efforts, focusing on minimizing interruptions in compressions and following protocols.

questions.answerText: Statements a and d are correct
questions.solution: p> Drug A has the highest efficacy with the highest potency. Drug B is more potent than drug C. Efficacy is the maximal effect a drug can produce, represented by the Vmax /y-axis value. The higher the Vmax, the higher the efficacy. Potency is the amount of drug required to produce a given effect. The lower the drug dose needed, the higher the potency. Both are independent of each other; efficacious drugs can have high or low potency and vice versa. The first graph helps us estimate the efficacy of the drugs (the higher the Vmax, the higher the efficacy). Thus, Drug A > B >C >D. The second graph helps us estimate the drugs' potency (The lower the drug dose needed, the higher the potency). The left shift of the graph indicates an increase in potency. Thus Drug D > B > C > A. @Neet_pg_bot

options.label: D

questions.solution: ng> Explanation: This scenario describes a Type II error, also known as a "false negative." Type II error occurs when we fail to reject a false null hypothesis. In this case, a potentially beneficial drug might be overlooked. Type II errors are particularly important in medical research, as they can lead to overlooking potentially beneficial treatments. The power of a statistical test (1 - probability of Type II error) is crucial in designing studies to minimise this risk. Type I error (Option A) occurs when you reject a true null hypothesis . @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: also known as primary systemic amyloidosis , is characterized by the deposition of amyloid fibrils derived from monoclonal immunoglobulin light chains (lambda or kappa) produced by clonal plasma cells. In this type of amyloidosis, the deposited amyloid fibrils can infiltrate various organs and tissues, including the kidneys, leading to organ dysfunction. Clinical manifestations commonly include Renal involvement causing proteinuria and renal impairment Hepatomegaly Peripheral oedema due to cardiac involvement. AA amyloidosis (Option A): AA amyloidosis, also known as secondary systemic amyloidosis, occurs secondary to chronic inflammatory conditions such as rheumatoid arthritis, inflammatory bowel disease, or chronic infections. In AA amyloidosis, the amyloid fibrils are derived from serum amyloid A protein, an acute-phase reactant synthesized predominantly by hepatocytes in response to inflammation. AB amyloidosis (Option B): AB amyloidosis is not a recognized subtype of amyloidosis. Amyloid fibrils derived from A Beta peptide are associated with Alzheimer's disease, but they are not a primary cause of systemic amyloidosis involving multiple organs. ATTR amyloidosis (Option D): ATTR amyloidosis, also known as transthyretin amyloidosis, occurs due to the deposition of amyloid fibrils derived from transthyretin protein, a transporter of thyroxine and retinol-binding protein. It can be hereditary (caused by mutations in the transthyretin gene) or acquired (due to wild-type transthyretin protein). It typically affects the heart and peripheral nerves, leading to cardiomyopathy and peripheral neuropathy, respectively. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 45-year-old male undergoes a split-thickness skin graft for a large wound on his leg. Three days postoperatively, the graft appears swollen with fluid accumulating underneath it. Which of the following complications is most likely?
questions.stemHtml: A 45-year-old male undergoes a split-thickness skin graft for a large wound on his leg. Three days postoperatively, the graft appears swollen with fluid accumulating underneath it. Which of the following complications is most likely?
questions.solution: ictid="84294069061692777198bdff94a950">seroma formation Explanation: In this scenario, the accumulation of fluid beneath the graft is indicative of hematoma or seroma formation. This complication can prevent proper adherence of the graft to the wound bed, leading to graft failure if not addressed promptly. Hematomas are collections of blood, while seromas are accumulations of clear fluid. Both can occur when there is inadequate hemostasis or when there is excessive movement or pressure on the graft site post-operatively. Complications of Skin Grafting: Graft Failure (Option A ruled out) : This occurs when the graft does not survive or integrate with the recipient site, due to poor vascularization or improper placement. It is not characterized by fluid accumulation beneath the graft. It can be prevented by ensuring good contact between the graft and the wound bed and avoiding movement or pressure on the graft. Infection (Option C ruled out) : Infection typically presents with redness, warmth, and pus rather than just fluid accumulation. Strict sterile techniques during surgery and the use of prophylactic antibiotics can help prevent infections. Hematoma or Seroma Formation (Option B) : Occur when blood or fluid collects under the graft. Proper hemostasis during surgery and the use of drains can prevent this issue. Poor Cosmetic Outcome (Option D ruled out) : If the graft does not match the recipient site's skin texture or thickness, or if it is not placed correctly, the cosmetic result may be unsatisfactory. Careful selection of graft thickness and meticulous placement can help achieve a better aesthetic outcome. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 45-year-old male patient has hypertension and hypokalemia. His blood pressure is consistently elevated despite being on multiple antihypertensive medications. Laboratory tests reveal elevated plasma aldosterone concentration and suppressed plasma renin activity. A CT scan of the abdomen shows an adrenal adenoma. Which is the most appropriate treatment for this patient's condition?
questions.stemHtml: A 45-year-old male patient has hypertension and hypokalemia. His blood pressure is consistently elevated despite being on multiple antihypertensive medications. Laboratory tests reveal elevated plasma aldosterone concentration and suppressed plasma renin activity. A CT scan of the abdomen shows an adrenal adenoma. Which is the most appropriate treatment for this patient's condition?
questions.solution: class="customMeta" data-dictid="982551b8f81692777189e20f09de85">hyperaldosteronism (Conn's syndrome) is characterised by excessive production of aldosterone from the adrenal glands, leading to hypertension and hypokalemia. Spironolactone, an aldosterone antagonist and a potassium-sparing diuretic, is the most appropriate drug of choice. Spironolactone: Aldosterone combines with an intracellular mineralocorticoid (MR) receptor and induces the formation of aldosterone-induced proteins (AIPs), which promote Na + reabsorption. Spironolactone acts as a competitive antagonist and inhibits the formation of AIP by combining with MR. This prevents aldosterone from promoting sodium reabsorption and potassium excretion, which are the primary mechanisms by which aldosterone increases blood pressure and causes hypokalemia. Lisinopril (Option A) is an angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitor that reduces aldosterone levels by inhibiting the production of angiotensin II. Hydrochlorothiazide (Option B) is a thiazide diuretic that inhibits the reabsorption of sodium and potassium; thus, hyperaldosteronism-induced hypokalemia will be worsened. Amlodipine (Option C) is a calcium channel blocker that works by relaxing the smooth muscle. @Neet_pg_bot

persistent pain, relieved by NSAIDs and an X-ray showing a characteristic lesion with a sclerotic margin and radiolucent nidus, points towards an Osteoid Osteoma.

 

Osteoid Osteoma

Demographics
  • Sex: Males > Females
  • Age: Young patients, but rare under 5 years and over 30.

Location
  • The diaphysis of long bones, especially the proximal tibia, and femur.
  • It can also occur in the spine, particularly the posterior arches.

Pathophysiology

The nidus releases prostaglandins which cause the characteristic pain that relieves on taking NSAIDs

Symptoms
  • Characterized by pain, often worse at night (Night crises), and relieved by NSAIDs (Therapeutic test).
  • When near joints, it may cause stiffness and effusion.
  • In the spine, it can lead to muscle spasms and scoliosis.

Radiology

X-Ray:

  • Dense sclerosis with a small, rounded area of osteolysis, often obscured by the surrounding sclerosis.
  • The characteristic lesion is less than 1.5 cm in diameter with a sclerotic margin and radiolucent nidus.

Isotope bone scans (Best investigation) are positive

Histology
  • Consists of a mesh of woven bone, osteoblastic rimming, osteoclasts, and dilated capillaries.
  • The mature osteoid forms the nidus, surrounded by dense, reactive bone and soft tissue with inflammatory changes.

Treatment
  • CT-guided radiofrequency ablation.
  • Surgical excision of the nidus (gold standard)

Management of Immune thrombocytopenic purpura in children.
